deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This is p.3 of Gauss's table on decomposing primes into three squares, 'Pars 3: numbers 8n+3' (previous page: 8k+1 and 8k+5). For each prime p = 8n+3 the entry gives:
(i) the order of the cyclic group of properly primitive classes of binary forms ax^2+2bxy+cy^2 of determinant b^2-ac = -p ('0,3' or '0.9' means the classes are indexed 0..2 or 0..8 by powers of a generator);
(ii) every essentially distinct decomposition p = a^2+b^2+c^2 ('Disc.' = discerptio);
(iii) for each decomposition, the class indices it corresponds to, written as inverse pairs k, -k ('Cl. 1.8' = classes g^1 and g^8);
(iv) after 'c:', the small primes (and 4) represented by forms of that class pair.
The header entry 3 = 1+1+1 is degenerate.

Numerically, the class count is h(-4p) = 3h(-p) for p ≡ 3 mod 8 (my statement). This gives 3 for p = 11, 19, 43, 67 (h(-p)=1) and 9 for p = 59, 83 (h(-p)=3).

THE STRUCTURE GAUSS RECORDS. A decomposition with two equal squares (11 = 9+1+1, 19 = 9+9+1, 43 = 25+9+9, 59 = 25+25+9, 67 = 49+9+9, 83 = 81+1+1) gives the principal class 0 together with the pair of order-3 classes ({1,2} when h=3; {3,6} when h=9). A decomposition with three distinct squares (59 = 49+9+1, 83 = 49+25+9) gives the six classes {1,8}, {2,7}, {4,5}.

In modern terms (my interpretation): each decomposition yields a coset C of the order-3 subgroup {0,3,6}, together with -C. Here {0,3,6} is the kernel of Cl(-4p) -> Cl(-p). For example {1,4,7} ∪ {8,5,2} = {1,8} ∪ {4,5} ∪ {2,7}.

This matches the count r_3(p) = 24 h(-p): 72 representations for 59 and 83, i.e. 8 per class. It also matches the rule on the previous page, '6n-3 indices, 3n-1 class pairs' (n = number of decompositions). For 59 (n=2) that is 9 indices and 5 pair entries. The next page (131, 179) shows the same pattern with cosets of {0,5,10} in Z/15.

REDUCED FORMS (my reconstruction):
- det -11: (1,0,11), (3,±1,4).
- det -19: (1,0,19), (4,±1,5).
- det -67: (1,0,67), (4,±1,17).
- det -59: (1,0,59), (3,±1,20) = index ±1, (7,±2,9) = ±2, (4,±1,15) = ±3, (5,±1,12) = ±4. Check: (3,1,20)^2 ~ (9,-4,7) ~ (7,2,9).
- det -83: (1,0,83), (3,±1,28) = ±1, (9,±4,11) = ±2, (4,±1,21) = ±3, (7,±1,12) = ±4. Check: (3,1,28)^2 ~ (9,8,11) in ax^2+bxy+cy^2 notation.

REPRESENTED PRIMES (checked by me):
- p=11. Principal: 47 = 36+11, 53 = 9+44. (3,1,4) gives 3, 4, 5, 23, 37, 59, 67, 71, 89.
- p=19. Principal: 23, 83. (4,1,5) gives 4, 5, 7, 11, 17, 43, 47, 61, 73. This list is complete below 100.
- p=43. Only 1 is entered; the class 1.2 list is left blank, so the entry is unfinished.
- p=59. Cl0: 1. Cl3.6: 4, 17, 71 (by 4x^2+2xy+15y^2). Cl1.8: 3, 41, 53. Cl2.7: 7, 29. Cl4.5: 5, 19.
- p=67. Principal: 71, 83. Cl1.2: the remaining primes below 100 with (q/67)=1. Complete and correct.
- p=83. Cl0: 1, 227 = 144+83 (no principal prime below 100). Cl3.6: 4, 23. Cl1.8: 3, 29. Cl2.7: 11, 31, 37 (via 9x^2+8xy+11y^2). Cl4.5: 7, 17.
errors: p=11: the decomposition is 9+1+1 (sum 11); '9+2+2' in the transcription is a misreading.

p=11, class pair 1.2: the list omits 31 = 3*9 - 12 + 16 (x=-3, y=2 in 3x^2+2xy+4y^2) and 97 (x=-3, y=5). Both satisfy (-11/q)=1 and are not of the form x^2+11y^2, so the list is incomplete although 89 is included.

p=59: 79 is placed in Cl.3.6, but 4x^2+2xy+15y^2 does not represent 79, whereas 3x^2+2xy+20y^2 does (x=-1, y=2: 3-4+80). So 79 belongs to Cl.1.8, the same pair as 3. The bold overwritten mark near '71.79' in the image may reflect a correction.
p=43: unfinished. Cl.0 should also list 47, 59, 79. Cl.1.2 (blank) would be 4, 11, 13, 17, 23, 31, 41, 53, 67, 83, 97.
p=83: the lists are partial. 41 (in Cl.3.6: 4*4+2*2+21), 59 and 61 are missing, although 59 and 61 satisfy (q/83)=1.

results.what: For p ≡ 3 mod 8, the number of properly primitive classes of determinant -p is 3 times the class number of discriminant -p (3, 3, 3, 9, 3, 9 for the primes here).
results.modern_name: Relation h(-4p) = 3h(-p) for p ≡ 3 mod 8 (class number of an order of conductor 2)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), arts. 253-256; later Dirichlet

results.what: Each decomposition p = a^2+b^2+c^2 corresponds to a definite set of classes. Two equal squares give the principal class and the order-3 classes; three distinct squares give a coset of the order-3 subgroup together with its inverse. The number of class pairs is 3n-1 from n decompositions.
results.modern_name: Gauss correspondence between primitive representations by x^2+y^2+z^2 and classes of binary forms of discriminant -4p; orbits under the kernel of Cl(-4p) -> Cl(-p) (cf. r_3(p) = 24h(-p) and the class-group action on sums of three squares)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, DA art. 291-292 (count); the explicit group-action/coset formulation is usually attributed to modern treatments (e.g. Venkov, Shemanske, Bhargava-style composition)

results.what: Tables of small primes represented by each class pair of determinant -p.
results.modern_name: Splitting of primes in ring class fields / representation of primes by binary quadratic forms

deep.surprise_reason: The counts (3h relation, r_3 = 24h) are Gauss's published results. The page goes further: it records explicitly that the classes attached to one three-square decomposition form a coset of the order-3 kernel subgroup (indices 0,3,6 versus 1,4,7 and their inverses), i.e. an empirical group-theoretic description of the representation-to-class map. That is a notable unpublished detail anticipating modern formulations, but it is close to what is implicit in DA arts. 291-292.
